title: Vocabulary Building
in30Seconds: Vocabulary is the set of words you know and use, and it is key to reading comprehension: you cannot understand a text without knowing what most of its words mean. You can grow it deliberately. Meet new words while reading and listening, understand them with dictionaries and word parts, use them in your own sentences, and review them from a word journal. Learn words in chunks and word families, not in isolation. A few words used well beat a long list memorized once.
whyItMatters: Every sentence you read, hear, write, or speak is built from words, so the size and precision of your word knowledge shapes how well you understand others and how clearly you express yourself. Reading specialists describe vocabulary as key to comprehension — readers cannot understand a text without knowing what most of its words mean. Because most words are learned indirectly through wide reading and listening, everyday input already grows your vocabulary; deliberate habits — noticing new words, learning their parts, recording them, and reviewing them — make that growth faster and more reliable. These habits carry over to lectures, textbooks, workplaces, and conversations, and they prepare you for later topics such as academic vocabulary and reading comprehension.
learningObjectives: Explain why vocabulary knowledge is central to reading comprehension.
Apply the word-learning cycle — encounter, understand, use, and review — to a new word.
Distinguish collocations and word families from isolated single words, using original examples.
Analyze words into roots, prefixes, and suffixes to see how word families are built.
Distinguish high-frequency, academic, and technical vocabulary and explain how the categories guide learning effort.

collegeVersion.heading: Why vocabulary deserves deliberate attention
collegeVersion.body: Vocabulary knowledge is central to reading comprehension. Reading specialists put it plainly: readers cannot understand what they are reading without knowing what most of the words mean. The same logic extends to listening, writing, and speaking — every act of communication runs on word knowledge. Research on vocabulary instruction shows that most words are learned indirectly, through daily encounters with spoken and written language, while some words must be taught directly. Wide reading and listening therefore do most of the work; deliberate attention does the rest, and it matters most for exactly the words that do not show up often enough to teach themselves.

collegeVersion.heading: The word-learning cycle
collegeVersion.body: A practical framework for deliberate growth has four steps: encounter, understand, use, and review. You encounter a new word in something you read or hear; understanding comes when you check its meaning — in a dictionary, from its word parts, or from the surrounding text; use means putting the word into your own speaking and writing, which turns passive recognition into active command; review means coming back to the word later, because a single meeting rarely sticks. The steps feed one another: each use and review strengthens the next encounter. The cycle also matches how reading research describes learning — most vocabulary grows through repeated encounters with language, and recording words and revisiting them supports memory.

collegeVersion.heading: Words in chunks: collocations and phrases
collegeVersion.body: Words rarely travel alone. A collocation is a combination of words that are often used together in a way that sounds natural: speakers say make a decision, not do a decision; heavy traffic, not weighty traffic; catch a cold, not receive a cold. Collocations range from fixed, where there is little choice about the partner word, to freer, where more options exist. Learning a word together with its usual partners is more useful than learning it alone, because that is the shape in which the word actually appears. Teachers recommend recording collocations in a notebook — the word, its partners, and an example sentence — so that each entry shows the word at work.

collegeVersion.heading: Word families and word parts
collegeVersion.body: English words are built from parts. The base word, or root, carries the core meaning; prefixes attach to the front and change the meaning — un- reverses or negates (unkind, unlock), re- means again (rebuild, retell), dis- reverses (disconnect, disagree), and inter- means between (intercity, international). Suffixes attach to the end and usually change the meaning or the part of speech: -tion often turns verbs into nouns (celebrate becomes celebration, inform becomes information), and -ful often turns words into adjectives (care becomes careful, colour becomes colourful). Words built from the same base form a family: view, viewer, review, and preview all carry the idea of seeing. Recognizing parts multiplies the words you can figure out, because morphology — how words are built from roots, prefixes, and suffixes — shows how words relate to one another.

collegeVersion.heading: High-frequency, academic, and technical words
collegeVersion.body: Vocabulary is often described in layers. High-frequency words — the everyday core such as book, eat, and happy — do most of the work in ordinary conversation and general reading. Academic words appear across many school and workplace subjects: the Academic Word List, developed by Averil Coxhead, contains 570 word families that sit outside the most frequent 2,000 words of English and were chosen as the words learners most need for tertiary study. Technical words belong to one field, such as photosynthesis in biology or leverage in finance, and word lists are also built for specific purposes, such as English for particular professions. The layers guide where to spend effort: the everyday core comes first, academic words repay attention as your study deepens — a topic of its own lesson — and technical words matter most inside their own fields.

collegeVersion.heading: Tools and habits: dictionaries, word journals, and realistic review
collegeVersion.body: Two tools make the cycle practical. A good learner's dictionary gives the meaning, the part of speech, pronunciation, and example sentences, and it records which words travel together. A word journal is your personal record: for each new word, note the meaning in your own words, a sentence that shows the word at work, its usual partners, and its word-family relatives. Realistic goals beat heroic ones — a small number of words used and reviewed beats a long list skimmed once. Review is the step learners skip most often, yet it is where memory is won: revisiting words after a few days, then again later, a habit often called spaced repetition, supports remembering far better than a single cramming session. Build the habit into your week, and let reading supply the encounters.

vocabulary.definition: The words a person knows and uses, including words recognized when reading or listening and words produced when speaking or writing.
A four-step loop for learning a word deliberately: encounter it, understand its meaning, use it yourself, and review it later.
A combination of words that are often used together so that the pairing sounds natural, such as make a decision or heavy traffic.
A group of words built from the same base word with different prefixes and suffixes, such as view, viewer, review, and preview.
The core part of a word to which prefixes and suffixes attach, such as view in review or act in react.
An affix attached to the beginning of a base word that changes its meaning, such as re- in rebuild or un- in unkind.
An affix attached to the end of a base word that usually changes its meaning or part of speech, such as -tion in celebration or -ful in careful.
The study of how words are built from roots, prefixes, and suffixes, and of how words relate to one another.
Words that appear across many school and workplace subjects, distinct from everyday high-frequency words and from field-specific technical terms.
A personal notebook in which a learner records new words with meanings, example sentences, usual partners, and related forms.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Your vocabulary is the set of words you know, and it does a huge job: you cannot understand a text without knowing what most of its words mean. The good news is that you are already learning words all the time — mostly without trying, through everything you read and hear. To grow on purpose, run a simple loop: meet a new word, figure out what it means, use it in a sentence of your own, and come back to it later. Learn words with their friends: make a decision and heavy traffic stick better than decision and traffic alone. Look inside the word too — un- flips meaning (unkind), re- means again (rebuild), -tion makes nouns (celebration), -ful makes adjectives (careful) — and whole families follow from one base (view, viewer, review). Keep a small journal, review it after a few days, and let reading supply new words. A few words you actually use beat a long list you met once.
eli10.analogy: Think of your vocabulary as a toolbox you carry everywhere. Reading and listening drop new tools into it for free; the cycle — encounter, understand, use, review — is you taking each tool out, checking what it is for, using it, and putting it back in a spot you will remember. Words learned in chunks are the multi-tools: one entry, many uses.
eli10.analogyLimits: The toolbox analogy has limits. A tool does not change meaning depending on the job, but a word can shift meaning with context, and word parts do not always add up neatly. Unlike a tool you can grab once, a word needs repeated use and review before it is truly yours.

workedExample: Meet the word sustainable in a news article: "The report argues that the current farming methods are not sustainable." Encounter: you have seen the word before but could not define it. Understand: the dictionary says able to continue without being exhausted or damaged, and the word parts agree — sustain, meaning to keep going or support, plus the suffix -able, meaning able to. Use: you write in your journal, "sustainable — able to keep going; our library's plan to buy used furniture is sustainable," and you note the family: sustain, sustained, sustainable, sustainability. Review: three days later you reread the entry, and that weekend you use the word in a conversation about the cost of textbooks. Encounter, understand, use, review — the same word has moved from unknown to usable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Learning words from long alphabetical lists.
commonMistakes.correction: Words memorized without context rarely stick or transfer. Learn words in chunks and sentences instead, and let reading and listening supply most encounters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Studying words one at a time, in isolation.
commonMistakes.correction: A word's partners and relatives carry much of its use. Record collocations such as make a decision and family members such as decide, decision, and decisive alongside the word.

commonMistakes.mistake: Looking a word up and never meeting it again.
commonMistakes.correction: A single dictionary check is only the understand step. Use the word in a sentence and review it from your journal, or the encounter fades.
Words like unkind, rebuild, and celebration look harder than they are. Recognizing un-, re-, dis-, -tion, and -ful lets one known base unlock many words.
Aiming for fifty words a day usually produces fifty forgotten words. A few words used and reviewed over several days outweigh a long list met once.

compareContrast.distinction: High-frequency words are the everyday core (book, eat, happy) that carries most ordinary communication; academic words such as analyse and methodology appear across many school and workplace subjects and are covered in their own lesson.

Academic words show up across many fields — methodology appears in science, business, and history papers alike — while technical words belong to one field, such as photosynthesis in biology or leverage in finance.
A single word learned alone, such as decision, gives you a label; the collocation make a decision gives you the word in the shape it actually appears in, which is how speakers expect to meet it.
Encountering a word means meeting it in reading or listening; reviewing means returning to it later. Encounter supplies the raw material, and review is what turns a meeting into a memory.

keyTakeaway: Vocabulary is key to comprehension, and it grows fastest when you make it deliberate: learn words in chunks and families, and move each new word through the cycle of encounter, understand, use, and review.

options: A combination of words that are often used together in a way that sounds natural
A word formed by joining a prefix and a suffix to a root
A sentence that defines an unfamiliar word directly
A group of words built from the same base word
questionBank.explanation: A collocation is a habitual pairing such as make a decision or heavy traffic, which is how the dictionary defines the term. Forming words from parts, defining words in sentences, and grouping words by a shared base are related but different ideas.

questionBank.prompt: Which group of words forms a word family built from the same base?
questionBank.explanation: View is the shared base: viewer adds the suffix -er, review adds the prefix re-, and preview adds pre-. The other options are comparative forms of one adjective, a list of fruits, or forms of a single verb — not a family built from one base with affixes.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing a word family built from one base

questionBank.prompt: If you know that the prefix re- means "again," which word most likely means "to build again"?
questionBank.explanation: Re- attaches to the front of the base build and signals doing it again, so rebuild means to build again. Un- reverses or negates, pre- means before, and sub- means under or below — none of which fits doing the action again.
questionBank.skill: Applying prefix knowledge to infer a word's meaning

questionBank.prompt: A learner reads the word "sustainable" in a report, checks its meaning in a dictionary, and writes a sentence of her own using it. Which step of the word-learning cycle is still missing?
questionBank.explanation: Reading the word is the encounter, the dictionary check is understanding, and her own sentence is use. The cycle is incomplete until she returns to the word later, because review is what turns a single meeting into a lasting memory.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing the word-learning cycle for a missing step

questionBank.prompt: Which word belongs to the high-frequency core of English rather than to academic or technical vocabulary?
questionBank.explanation: Kitchen is part of the everyday core that carries ordinary conversation and general reading. Photosynthesis is a field-specific science term, while methodology and analyse are academic words of the kind the Academic Word List collects because they appear across school and workplace subjects.
questionBank.skill: Classifying words as high-frequency, academic, or technical
